# Government Benefits Portal — Pre-VPAT Accessibility Audit Plan > **For Claude:** Use a11y-planner protocol. Review with a11y-critic at the checkpoints defined below. > **Compliance target:** WCAG 2.2 Level AA (see §1.2 — the *legal* baseline may be WCAG 2.1 AA; 2.2 AA is a superset and remains the working target) > **Users who need accessibility:** Screen reader users, keyboard-only users, low-vision / magnification users, voice-input users, users with cognitive and learning disabilities, users on low-end Android devices, deaf and hard-of-hearing users (video content) > **Assistive technologies:** NVDA + Chrome/Firefox, JAWS + Chrome, VoiceOver + Safari (macOS), iOS VoiceOver + Safari, TalkBack + Chrome (Android), Dragon NaturallySpeaking, Windows Magnifier, forced-colors / High Contrast mode, keyboard-only **Feature:** A systematic, WCAG-EM–based conformance evaluation of a 20-page government benefits portal, producing an accurate VPAT/ACR and a prioritized remediation backlog within 13 weeks. **Risk Level:** **High** — multi-page authenticated process, legal/financial transactions, statutory compliance exposure, published conformance claim. **Component Type:** Site-level audit methodology (not a single-component build plan). The deliverable is an executable test methodology plus the pass/fail specifications a QA engineer needs to judge each shared component. --- ## 1. Scope & Context ### 1.1 What is being planned, and why An audit *methodology*, not an audit *result*. This plan tells two QA engineers with basic accessibility knowledge: which pages to test, in what order, with which tools, against which explicit pass criteria, how to record findings, how to rank them, and how those findings become rows in a published VPAT. The user need is unusually concrete: this portal is how citizens apply for public assistance. An inaccessible step in the application flow does not degrade an experience — it denies a benefit. That framing drives every prioritization decision below. ### 1.2 Legal and standards baseline — resolve this before anything else The brief says "government benefits portal" and "WCAG 2.2 AA" without identifying the obligated entity. The legal baseline differs materially: | Entity type | Governing rule | Referenced standard | Deadline | |---|---|---|---| | Federal agency / federal procurement | Revised Section 508 (36 CFR 1194, Appendix A), E205.4 | WCAG 2.0 Level A + AA incorporated by reference | In force | | State or local government | ADA Title II web rule (28 CFR part 35, subpart H) | WCAG 2.1 Level AA | Entities serving population ≥50,000: **April 2026 — already elapsed as of this plan's date.** Smaller entities and special districts: April 2027 | **Action:** confirm the entity classification in Week 1 and record it in the VPAT's "Applicable Standards/Guidelines" section. If this is a state/local entity of ≥50,000 population, the compliance date has passed and the audit is remediating an existing exposure, not preparing for a future one — which changes how CRITICAL findings are escalated and how the remediation roadmap must be worded. Targeting **WCAG 2.2 AA** is correct regardless: it is a superset of 2.1 AA (2.2 adds nine SC and obsoletes 4.1.1 Parsing), so conformance to 2.2 AA satisfies either baseline. Note that WCAG 2.2 additions are disproportionately relevant to this portal — see §7. ### 1.3 WCAG conformance requirements that constrain the sampling design These are not stylistic preferences; they determine what a defensible sample looks like. - **CR2 Full Pages** — conformance is claimed for *whole pages*. You cannot exclude the reCAPTCHA widget or the YouTube embed from a page's conformance verdict just because you did not author them. See §12. - **CR3 Complete Processes** — if a page is part of a multi-page process, *every* page in that process must conform for the process to conform. The 6-step application, plus account creation, login, upload, and confirmation, are therefore **not samplable**. All of them are in the sample. This single requirement is why authenticated flows are Tier 1. - **CR5 Non-Interference** — 1.4.2 Audio Control, 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap, 2.2.2 Pause/Stop/Hide, and 2.3.1 Three Flashes apply to *all* content on a page, including third-party content, even content that is not otherwise part of the conformance claim. A keyboard trap inside a third-party widget fails the page. ### 1.4 Capacity arithmetic — is 13 weeks with 2 engineers real? Stating this openly because the plan is worthless if the timeline is fiction. | Work package | Estimate | |---|---| | Automated baseline across ~50 page-states + incomplete-result triage | ~60 h | | Shared component deep audit (8 patterns × keyboard + DOM + 2 SRs) | ~80 h | | Tier 1 authenticated journey (≈28 page-states × ~4.5 h manual + SR) | ~126 h | | Tier 3/4 public pages (≈14 page-states × ~2 h) | ~28 h | | Cross-cutting passes (reflow, forced colors, motion, voice, magnification) | ~60 h | | Re-test and regression after remediation | ~100 h | | VPAT drafting, evidence assembly, reconciliation | ~60 h | | **Total** | **≈515 h** | Two engineers at ~25 genuinely-productive audit hours per week × 13 weeks ≈ 650 h. It fits, with roughly 20% buffer — **but only under three conditions**: 1. **Remediation is staffed separately.** The 515 h contains zero development hours. If the QA pair is also expected to fix findings, the plan fails. 2. **Shared-component findings ship to developers in Week 3–5, not at the end.** Sequential audit-then-fix does not fit in 13 weeks. 3. **Re-test is scoped to changed surfaces plus a regression sweep**, not a full second audit. If any condition cannot be met, the honest response is to publish an accurate VPAT with open "Does Not Support" rows and a dated remediation roadmap — not to compress the audit. See §19. ### 1.5 Existing code The site is live and four years old, server-rendered HTML with progressive JavaScript enhancement (no SPA framework). Two consequences: - **Good:** no client-side routing means no SPA focus-loss-on-navigation class of defect, and no virtual-DOM re-render focus destruction. Native page loads move focus to the document correctly by default. - **Risk:** four years of incremental fixes on a server-rendered template system typically produces *partial* selector coverage — a fix applied to one template variant and not its siblings. Known Pitfall #5 in the planner protocol. The three Program Detail variants exist precisely to expose this, and are deliberately kept in the sample for that reason. Because the site is live, every finding must cite the URL, the page state, and a resolvable selector — see the defect record contract in §14. ### 1.6 Constraints - 13 weeks to VPAT publication. - 2 QA engineers. - axe DevTools Enterprise already licensed (use it; do not propose replacing it). - Government compliance documentation required. - Template: "ITI VPAT® 2.4 Rev, Section 508 edition" (the brief writes "ITTF"; the publisher is the Information Technology Industry Council — correct the attribution in the document header). **Verify in Week 1 that the chosen edition's WCAG tables cover WCAG 2.2.** VPAT 2.4Rev's tables were authored against earlier WCAG versions, and ITI has published later revisions adding the 2.2 criteria. If the 2.4Rev tables stop at 2.1, either upgrade the template or append the nine 2.2 criteria as a clearly-labelled supplementary table. Confidence: moderate on the exact edition history — treat this as a task, not a stated fact. ### 1.7 Scope questions that must be closed before the sample is frozen (Week 1) These are gaps in the brief, not in the plan. Each has a materially different answer depending on the resolution. 1. **The 8th shared component.** The brief scopes "8 shared component patterns" but names seven: mega-menu, search with live results, in-page alerts, data tables, file upload, date picker, session timeout modal. The inventory step must identify the eighth. Strong candidates: the form validation / error-summary pattern (arguably the single highest-risk shared pattern here), the FAQ accordion, site footer, or pagination. Do not proceed with an unnamed slot. 2. **PDFs and non-web documents.** Benefits portals invariably serve PDF notices, determination letters, and printable application forms. The brief lists none. Under Section 508 these are electronic content and are in scope; for a VPAT they need their own evaluation. **Resolve explicitly**: either bring a sampled set of PDFs into scope (add ~40 h) or state their exclusion in the VPAT's Evaluation Methods section. Silently omitting them produces an incomplete conformance claim. 3. **Transactional email and the Notification Center.** Are notification emails in scope, or only the in-portal Notification Center? 4. **Authenticated test data.** The audit cannot start without seeded accounts parked at each application step, uploadable test documents, populated application-history rows, and both empty and populated notification states. This is the most common cause of audit slippage in week 2. 5. **reCAPTCHA and automation.** reCAPTCHA v2 on login will block scripted Playwright runs. Google publishes test site/secret keys that always pass; the test environment must be configured with them, or the environment allowlisted. Resolve in Week 1 or the entire automated authenticated lane stalls. 6. **Native mobile app.** Assumed out of scope. Confirm — if one exists, it needs its own VPAT tables (Chapter 5 Software). --- ## 2. Evaluation Methodology — WCAG-EM The sampling and reporting framework is **WCAG-EM**, the W3C's own conformance evaluation methodology. Use whichever version the organization adopts: - **WCAG-EM 1.0** — "Website Accessibility Conformance Evaluation Methodology (WCAG-EM) 1.0", W3C Working Group Note, 2014. - **WCAG-EM 2.0** — "WCAG Evaluation Methodology", W3C Group Note, 2026, which broadens the framing from *websites* to *digital products*. Either is defensible; 1.0 is the version most procurement reviewers and legal teams will recognize, so unless the organization has already adopted 2.0, **use 1.0 and cite it by name in the VPAT's Evaluation Methods section.** Naming a published methodology is what distinguishes an auditable conformance claim from an assertion. ### 2.1 The five WCAG-EM steps, mapped to this engagement | WCAG-EM step | This audit | |---|---| | **1. Define the Evaluation Scope** | §1.2 (standard + level), §1.7 (boundary questions), AT support baseline in §5.2, "conformance evaluated against the sample" statement | | **2. Explore the Target Website** | Week 1 crawl and inventory: all URLs, all templates, all shared components, all page states, all technologies (JS enhancements, iframes, third-party scripts). Produces the state inventory in §2.3 | | **3. Select a Representative Sample** | §2.3–2.5: structured sample + complete processes + randomly selected sample | | **4. Audit the Selected Sample** | §4–§11 (tools and per-component pass specifications), executed per §16 | | **5. Report the Evaluation Findings** | §14 (defect record), §15 (VPAT structure) | ### 2.2 The unit of test is the page *state*, not the page "20 pages" understates the surface by roughly 2.5×. A page with a closed mega-menu and a page with an open mega-menu are different accessibility trees. The inventory in Week 1 must enumerate states, and every automated scan runs per state. Expected inventory, approximately: | Surface | States | |---|---| | 20 named pages, default state | 20 | | Mega-menu expanded (canonical instance) | 1 | | Search: suggestions open, results populated, zero results | 3 | | Application steps 1–6, validation-error state each | 6 | | Application confirmation / submitted | 1 | | Login: error state; Account creation: error state | 2 | | File upload: idle, in-progress, success, rejected-file error | 4 | | Session timeout warning modal open | 1 | | Dashboard: empty, populated, sorted-descending | 3 | | Notification center: empty, populated, unread badge | 3 | | FAQ accordion expanded | 1 | | Date picker dialog open | 1 | | Site error states: 404, session expired | 2 | | **Approximate total machine-scannable states** | **≈48** | | **Of which warrant full manual + screen reader treatment** | **≈32** | ### 2.3 Structured sample — page tiers and rationale Testing all 20 pages to equal depth is both methodologically wrong and infeasible here. WCAG-EM sampling is risk- and coverage-driven. Tiers: | Tier | Pages | Depth | Rationale | |---|---|---|---| | **Tier 1 — Deep** | Login, Account creation, Application steps 1–6, Document upload, Application status dashboard, Notification center *(11 pages, ≈28 states)* | Automated per state + full manual keyboard + DOM reference verification + 2 desktop SRs + 1 mobile SR on the end-to-end process + voice-input pass + reflow | WCAG CR3 forbids sampling within a complete process. Highest user consequence: failure here denies a benefit. Highest JS density. Legal/financial data triggers WCAG 3.3.4 | | **Tier 2 — Shared components** | Mega-menu, search + live results, alerts/notifications, data table, file upload, date picker, session timeout modal, + the unidentified 8th *(8 patterns)* | Full manual + DOM verification + 2 desktop SRs, tested once in a canonical host page, then **presence-and-parity verified** on every other page where they appear | Highest leverage in the plan — one fix propagates to all 20 pages. See §2.6 | | **Tier 3 — Standard** | Program Listings, Program Detail ×3, FAQ, News, Contact *(7 pages)* | Automated per state + manual keyboard + 1 desktop SR spot check + media review on video pages | Real content variety, real template divergence risk (the three Program Detail variants), reCAPTCHA on Contact, YouTube on Program pages | | **Tier 4 — Light** | Home, About *(2 pages)* | Automated + manual keyboard + structural review | Lowest unique-content risk. **Caveat:** Home is the canonical host for the mega-menu and search, so it receives full Tier 2 treatment for those components. Its *unique* content is what is light-touch | ### 2.4 Complete-process coverage (non-negotiable) The end-to-end journey — **Account creation → Login → Application step 1 … step 6 → Document upload → Confirmation → Status dashboard → Notification** — is audited as one continuous process, by one engineer, in one session, once per assistive technology. Not page-by-page in isolation. Process-level defects (state lost between steps, focus not reset on step change, progress indicator not announced, WCAG 3.3.7 Redundant Entry violations) are invisible to page-by-page testing. Run this journey a minimum of four times: JAWS+Chrome, NVDA+Chrome, iOS VoiceOver+Safari, TalkBack+Chrome. ### 2.5 Randomly selected sample WCAG-EM prescribes an additional **randomly selected** sample — commonly around 10% of the structured sample size — drawn from the full URL inventory rather than from the curated list. Its purpose is to catch what curation misses. **Method:** after the Week 1 crawl produces the complete URL inventory, seed a random number generator with a recorded seed, draw 3–5 URLs, and record the seed and the drawn URLs in the VPAT. A reproducible seed is what makes the random sample auditable rather than decorative. If a randomly drawn page reveals a defect class absent from the structured sample, that is a signal the structured sample is under-representative — expand it. ### 2.6 Shared component leverage — the efficiency that makes 13 weeks work The single most important economic fact of this audit: **a defect in the mega-menu is one defect, not twenty.** Auditing each page as a standalone artifact would re-discover the same nav defect 20 times, consume the entire budget on rediscovery, and generate a remediation backlog that misleads developers about actual effort. The operating rule: 1. Audit each shared component **once, deeply**, in a canonical host page. 2. Record the finding once, with a **site-wide reach flag** and the list of pages where the component appears. 3. On every other page, run only a **parity check**: is this the same component instance, same markup, same behavior? Parity checks take minutes, not hours. 4. **Parity checks are where four years of incremental fixes get caught.** Expect at least one component to diverge across templates — most likely the mega-menu across the three Program Detail variants, or the alert pattern between public and authenticated shells. A parity failure is its own finding. 5. Remediation of Tier 2 components is sequenced **first**, so the fix lands before the re-test window. --- ## 3. Per planner Pitfall #1: **one announcement region per event class, page-level and persistent** — never `role="alert"` inside a repeating template or loop. Per-field error text is associated with its input via `aria-describedby`, not via its own live region. --- ## 4. The APG is explicit that Menu/Menubar models *application* menus and imposes an arrow-key navigation model that site navigation does not follow; applying it to a link list makes JAWS and NVDA enter a mode where Tab no longer behaves as users expect and links are announced as "menu item" rather than "link". If the audit finds `role="menu"` on site navigation, the finding is a 4.1.2 failure with a MAJOR-to-CRITICAL severity depending on whether links remain reachable. Also test explicitly: **hover-triggered and click/focus-triggered branches both** (Pitfall #4). Mega-menus that open on hover frequently have no keyboard path at all, or have a keyboard path that never closes. Enumerate every open/close trigger — hover in, hover out, click, Enter, Space, Escape, focus-out, click-outside, viewport resize into mobile breakpoint — and test each. **Search with live results — classify before testing.** "Search with live results" is ambiguous and the correct pattern differs completely between the two readings. Step one of this component's audit is a classification decision: (a) autocomplete suggestions in a popup → Combobox pattern applies, `aria-activedescendant` and `aria-expanded` are required; (b) results rendered into the page below the input → Combobox is *wrong*, and applying it would be a false finding. Record the classification in the defect record so the reviewer's reasoning is auditable. **Session timeout modal — WCAG 2.2.1 is the substance, not the ARIA.** A perfectly-marked-up `alertdialog` that gives the user 20 seconds to react still fails 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable. The criterion requires one of: turn off, adjust to at least 10× the default, or extend with a simple action after a warning of at least 20 seconds. For a benefits application where a user may be gathering documents mid-form, this is a genuine data-loss risk, not a technicality. Test it by leaving a half-completed application idle and observing what happens to entered data. If data is lost on timeout, that is CRITICAL regardless of the modal's ARIA quality. **Date picker — test with Dragon, not just a keyboard.** Custom date grids are the classic voice-input failure: there is nothing to say. Confirm the text input remains directly typable and that the format is stated in text associated via `aria-describedby` (WCAG 3.3.2), e.g. "Date of birth, format MM/DD/YYYY". --- ## 5. Tool Selection & Rationale ### 5.1 Tool roles — complementary, never substitutable | Tool | Role | What it uniquely provides | What it cannot do | |---|---|---|---| | **axe DevTools Enterprise / axe-core** | Primary automated rule engine; the CI-integrated pass/fail gate | Deterministic, versioned, low-false-positive rule results with element selectors; scales across ~48 page-states; Enterprise adds Intelligent Guided Tests (structured semi-manual flows for keyboard, modals, structure) which suit a 2-person team | Cannot judge focus order quality, whether an announcement actually occurred, whether alt text is *correct*, whether an error message is *useful*, or anything inside a cross-origin iframe | | **WAVE** | Human structural read of a single page | Renders headings, landmarks, ARIA, and reading order as an on-page overlay, so a reviewer *sees* structure rather than reading a JSON report. Fast triage of "is this page's outline sane" | Not a scalable scanner; different rule set and different naming from axe. **Do not treat WAVE and axe as interchangeable.** Findings must be reconciled to a single WCAG SC, not double-counted | | **Manual keyboard testing** | The only method for focus order, focus traps, focus restoration, focus visibility, 2.4.11 | Everything about focus. Nothing automated substitutes for it | Slow; requires discipline and a scripted procedure to be repeatable across two engineers | | **Screen readers (NVDA, JAWS, VO, iOS VO, TalkBack)** | Verification of name/role/state and actual announcements | The only evidence that a live region announced, that a name is comprehensible, that reading order is usable | Behavior differs per SR/browser pair; a JAWS-only finding is not automatically a WCAG failure — see §5.4 | | **Lighthouse** | Trend smoke signal only | Cheap, already in Chrome | **Banned from the VPAT.** It runs a subset of axe-core and produces a weighted 0–100 score. Nothing else. - Result types retained: `violations` **and** `incomplete`. Incomplete results are not passes — they are the manual queue, and dropping them is the most common way an automated baseline understates a site. - Frame traversal enabled for same-origin iframes. - No `disableRules`. Best-practice findings are not SC failures and must never appear in a conformance table. **Scoping:** - Third-party regions (reCAPTCHA iframe, YouTube iframe) are **excluded from the remediation backlog, not from the scan record.** Scan them, tag the results `third-party`, retain the evidence for the VPAT remarks. Cross-origin iframes cannot be traversed from the parent document at all — record those as "not machine-testable; manually evaluated" rather than as passes. - Component-scoped runs (`include` on the component root) for Tier 2 parity checks, so a mega-menu parity failure is not buried in whole-page noise. **Expected yield — calibrate the team's expectations.** Automated rule engines detect a minority of WCAG failures by count; published estimates commonly land in the 30–40% range, with vendors claiming more when guided/semi-manual tests are included. Treat any specific percentage as an estimate that varies by site, not a fact. The operational implication is fixed regardless of the exact number: **a clean axe run is the starting point of this audit, not evidence of conformance**, and the plan must not budget as though automation is doing most of the work. ### 5.3 Playwright harness specification - **Authenticated state:** a global setup logs in once (with reCAPTCHA test keys) and persists `storageState`, reused by all authenticated specs. Avoids re-authenticating ~28 times and avoids CAPTCHA in the loop. - **State-variant scanning:** each spec drives the UI to a named state (open the menu; submit the form empty; start an upload; trigger the timeout modal) *then* runs the axe analysis. This is the mechanism that turns "20 pages" into "~48 states". - **Real keyboard events only:** `page.keyboard.press()`. Synthetic `dispatchEvent` is forbidden — it bypasses browser default behavior and produces tests that pass while the site is unusable. - **Focus assertions:** capture `document.activeElement` after each Tab and assert the resulting sequence against an expected ordered list of accessible names. This makes focus order a regression-testable artifact rather than a one-time manual observation. - **Reference integrity sweep (site-wide, cheap, high-yield):** walk every `aria-labelledby`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-controls`, `aria-owns`, and `label[for]` on the page and assert (a) every IDREF resolves to an existing element, (b) no duplicate `id` values exist in the document. On a four-year-old server-rendered site with loop-generated markup, broken IDREFs and duplicate IDs are near-certain, invisible to visual review, and silently break every association the developers believe they implemented. - **Live region instrumentation:** attach a MutationObserver to the page-level status and alert containers, and record what text was inserted and when. This is machine evidence that a change *would* be announced. **Honest limit:** it is not evidence that a screen reader *did* announce it — only the SR pass in §6.2 establishes that. - **Reflow check:** set viewport to 320 × 1024 (equivalent to 1280px at 400% zoom) and assert `documentElement.scrollWidth` does not exceed the viewport width beyond a small tolerance. ### 5.4 Reconciling tool disagreement Two engineers using four tools will produce conflicting findings. The rule: **a finding enters the VPAT only when it is expressed as a specific WCAG success criterion failure on a specific page, with evidence.** Tool output is input to that judgment, never the judgment itself. - axe violation with no identifiable SC failure → advisory, not a conformance row. - WAVE "alert" (its non-error category) → triage manually; most are advisory. - Behavior that differs between JAWS and NVDA → investigate the underlying markup. If the markup is spec-correct and one SR renders it poorly, that is an **AT bug**, documented in the VPAT remarks under the relevant criterion, not necessarily an SC failure. Say which SR and which version. "Screen readers announce this oddly" is not admissible evidence. --- ## 6. Every item below is manual. **Site-wide rules to verify on every page:** 1. Tab order matches visual reading order (WCAG 2.4.3); no positive `tabindex` anywhere. 2. Focus indicator visible on every focusable element, at every zoom level and in forced-colors mode (WCAG 2.4.7). The robust technique is **two-tone**: an `outline` plus a contrasting `box-shadow`, so the indicator survives against both light and dark backgrounds. Single-color outlines vanish when they match the element or page background. Use `:focus-visible`, not `:focus`. Inline elements produce fragmented outlines — `display: inline-block` fixes the rectangle. Framework CSS and browser defaults frequently override author focus styles at lower specificity; verify the *rendered* indicator, not the stylesheet. 3. **WCAG 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), AA — new in 2.2 and highly likely to fail here.** With a sticky header present, Tab through the page and confirm no focused element is *entirely* hidden behind the header, the cookie banner, or a sticky footer. This is a near-guaranteed finding on a four-year-old site with a sticky header, and it is invisible to every automated tool. 4. No keyboard trap anywhere (WCAG 2.1.2) — including inside the reCAPTCHA and YouTube iframes, which fall under CR5 Non-Interference. 5. `aria-hidden="true"` alone does **not** remove an element from the tab order. Verify that collapsed mega-menu panels, off-canvas mobile nav, and background content behind the timeout modal are made unfocusable via `inert`, `display:none`, `visibility:hidden`, or conditional server-side rendering — not by `aria-hidden` alone. Content Accessibility Test Specifications **Alt text (WCAG 1.1.1).** Decorative images `alt=""`; informative images concise and specific; complex images (benefit-eligibility charts, process diagrams) get a short `alt` plus a long description via `aria-describedby` or an adjacent text equivalent. Image links: alt text names the *destination*, not the image. **Planner Pitfall #8:** if a link already carries an `aria-label` or the image is `aria-hidden`, the image's `alt` must be empty — otherwise a decorative description is read alongside or instead of the link's actual purpose. **Icon fonts.** If the site uses Font Awesome, Material Icons, or Glyphicons, every decorative icon element needs `aria-hidden="true"`. An icon that is the *sole* content of a button or link is **not** decorative: the parent element needs an `aria-label`. For a site this size, a single runtime behavior that scans common icon selectors and applies `aria-hidden`, with detection for sole-content cases, is more reliable than template-by-template edits. **Link text (WCAG 2.4.4).** No bare "click here", "read more", "learn more", "apply". On the Program Listings page — where every card ends in "Learn more" — a screen reader user pulling up the links list hears eight identical entries. Fix with visually-hidden continuation text or `aria-label` that *contains* the visible text (so WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name still holds for voice users). Links opening a new window or launching a download must say so in text. **Accessible names — never `title`.** `title` produces a tooltip and is not a reliable accessible name across screen readers. Use a visible `<label>` or `aria-label`. **One legitimate exception:** the `title` attribute on `<iframe>` *is* the correct accessible-name mechanism for frames (WCAG technique H64) and is required on both the reCAPTCHA and YouTube iframes. A 4.1.2 failure that hides a submit button outranks a 1.4.3 failure in the footer, regardless of how the criteria sort numerically. | Severity | Definition | Examples on this portal | Remediation SLA | |---|---|---|---| | **CRITICAL** | Blocks completion of a user journey for at least one user group, with no workaround | Keyboard trap in the timeout modal; unlabeled required field in an application step; file upload with no keyboard path; session expiry that destroys entered data with no extension; a step whose Continue button is unreachable | Fix before VPAT publication. Escalate on discovery, do not batch | | **MAJOR** | Significant friction; a workaround exists but is burdensome, undiscoverable, or requires expertise | Error summary present but not focused after submit (user can hunt for errors); table sortable but sort state not announced; mega-menu opens on hover only but links remain reachable through a fallback; 8 identical "Learn more" links | Fix in this cycle | | **MINOR** | Inconvenience; the journey completes without significant added effort | Glyph read redundantly alongside `aria-expanded`; slightly verbose accessible name; a non-blocking duplicate ID | Fix if capacity allows; otherwise carry into the roadmap | | **ADVISORY** | Not a success-criterion failure. Best practice, usability, or AAA | 44×44 target sizes (AAA) not met though 24×24 is; AAA contrast; a missing reverse skip link on a moderate-length page | Recommendations appendix only. **Never enters a conformance table** | ### 12.1 The distinction that keeps the VPAT legally accurate **Severity and conformance are different axes and must not be merged.** - **Severity** drives the remediation backlog and the sprint order. - **Conformance verdict** ("Supports / Partially Supports / Does Not Support") is driven solely by: *is this a failure of this success criterion on this page?* A MINOR issue can be an unambiguous SC failure. If severity is allowed to drive the VPAT column, MINOR failures get quietly recorded as "Supports" and the VPAT becomes inaccurate — which, in a procurement context, is a misrepresentation. Enforce this at the defect-record level: severity and conformance verdict are two separate required fields, filled in independently, and the reviewer must be able to justify a "Supports" verdict on a page carrying an open MINOR finding for that same criterion (usually they cannot). ### 12.2 Remediation ordering Fix order is a function of three factors, not severity alone: ``` Rank = journey criticality × severity × reach ``` - **Journey criticality:** application flow > login/account > status/notifications > public content. - **Reach:** site-wide shared component > multi-page template > single page. The practical consequence: a **MAJOR defect in the mega-menu (site-wide, on the path to everything) is scheduled before a CRITICAL defect on the About page.** Shared-component fixes are also scheduled first for timeline reasons — they must land before the re-test window opens. --- ## 13. Defect Record & Execution Consistency ### 13.1 Required fields per finding Every finding, regardless of source tool, records: - **Stable ID** — deterministically derived from page URL + component + criterion + selector, so the same defect reconciles across the audit, the re-test, and the VPAT without manual matching. - **Page URL** and **page state** (e.g. "step 3, validation-error state"). - **Component** and **reach** (page-specific / template / site-wide, with the page list). - **Selector / XPath** to the failing element, plus the **HTML snippet**. - **WCAG SC + level** (single primary criterion; secondary criteria listed separately). - **Conformance verdict** for that criterion on that page. - **Severity** (independent field — §12.1). - **Detection method** — tool + version, or AT + version + browser + OS. - **Steps to reproduce**, **expected behavior**, **actual behavior**. - **Evidence** — screenshot, screen recording, or SR speech-viewer transcript. - **Remediation owner** and target date. No finding enters the VPAT without a criterion, a location, and reproduction steps. Findings that cannot state all three are observations, not findings. ### 13.2 Inter-rater calibration — the control that makes two engineers produce one audit Two engineers testing independently will disagree on SC attribution and severity. Unmanaged, this produces a VPAT that is internally inconsistent — the fastest way to lose credibility with a reviewer. **Week 1 calibration exercise (mandatory before independent work begins):** 1. Both engineers independently audit the same two pages — one Tier 1 (an application step) and one Tier 3 (Program Detail). 2. Compare findings: agreement on *existence*, on *SC attribution*, and on *severity*. 3. Reconcile every disagreement and write the resolution into a living decision log ("recurring adjudications"), covering at minimum: which criterion owns a missing label (1.3.1 vs 3.3.2 vs 4.1.2); when a contrast issue is 1.4.3 vs 1.4.11; when an SR-specific behavior is an AT bug rather than an SC failure; when an issue is MAJOR rather than CRITICAL. 4. **Gate:** proceed to independent work only at ≥80% agreement on SC attribution. Repeat on a second page pair if the gate is not met. 5. Repeat a lightweight calibration at the midpoint (Week 7) to catch drift. **Ongoing:** all CRITICAL findings, all third-party adjudications, and all "Supports" verdicts on pages carrying open findings receive a second-engineer review before entering the VPAT. --- ## 14. VPAT / ACR Reporting Structure The completed VPAT is an **Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR)**. Use the correct term in procurement contexts. ### 14.1 Document structure (ITI VPAT 2.4 Rev, Section 508 edition) 1. **Header** — product name and version, report date, contact information, notes, and **evaluation methods used**. The evaluation-methods block is where the audit's credibility lives: name WCAG-EM and its version; list every tool with version; list every AT with version, browser, and OS; give the audit date range; and **state explicitly that the evaluation was conducted against a defined sample, and enumerate the sampled URLs** (including the random-sample URLs and the reproducible seed). 2. **Applicable Standards/Guidelines** — WCAG 2.2 Level A and AA; Revised Section 508 (and/or the ADA Title II referenced standard, per §1.2). 3. **Terms** — Supports / Partially Supports / Does Not Support / Not Applicable / Not Evaluated. Per ITI convention, **"Not Evaluated" is permitted only for Level AAA**. Every AA criterion must carry a verdict. 4. **Table 1: Success Criteria, Level A** — all Level A criteria. 5. **Table 2: Success Criteria, Level AA** — all Level AA criteria, including the WCAG 2.2 additions: 2.4.11, 2.5.7, 2.5.8, 3.3.8 (plus Level A additions 3.2.6 and 3.3.7 in Table 1). 6. **Table 3: Level AAA** — optional; mark "Not Evaluated" throughout unless specific criteria were assessed. 7. **Chapter 3: Functional Performance Criteria** — often skipped and it should not be. These describe outcomes ("without vision", "with limited manipulation", "without hearing") and are where a reviewer looks to understand real-world usability. They must be consistent with Tables 1–2. 8. **Chapter 4: Hardware** — "Not Applicable" for a web portal, with a one-line rationale. 9. **Chapter 5: Software** — largely "Not Applicable" for web content; confirm whether any downloadable software or authoring capability is in scope. 10. **Chapter 6: Support Documentation and Services** — routinely forgotten. The portal's *own* help documentation, PDFs, and support channels must themselves be accessible. If help is delivered as untagged PDFs, that is a Chapter 6 gap. 11. **Legal disclaimer** and a link to the remediation roadmap. ### 14.2 Reporting rules - **4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete and removed in WCAG 2.2.** If the template still lists it, mark it per current ITI guidance (typically "Not Applicable" with a note that the criterion was removed in WCAG 2.2) rather than evaluating it. Never report a 4.1.1 failure in a 2.2 claim. - **Never leave "Partially Supports" unexplained.** The Remarks column must state *what* fails, *where*, and *what the user impact is*. An unexplained "Partially Supports" is the single most common defect in published VPATs and the first thing a procurement reviewer challenges. - **No Lighthouse scores. No "X% accessible."** Percentage-conformant is not a thing; conformance is per-criterion and per-page. - **The conformance claim is bounded by the sample.** Say so plainly in the evaluation-methods block. A blanket site-wide claim from a 20-page sample is unsupported. ### 14.3 Criteria most likely to fail — pre-load the reviewer's attention The WebAIM Million annual analysis consistently identifies the same top failures across large samples of home pages, and government portals of this age match the pattern. Expect these to dominate the automated yield: | Criterion | Typical manifestation here | |---|---| | **1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)** | Placeholder text, hint text, disabled controls, footer small print, status badges | | **1.1.1 Non-text Content** | Program icons, chart images, decorative images with descriptive alt | | **4.1.2 Name, Role, Value** | Icon-only buttons (dismiss, sort, upload), custom widgets | | **2.4.4 / 4.1.2** | Empty or duplicate links — the "Learn more" cluster | | **1.3.1 Info and Relationships** | Missing labels, missing `<th scope>`, headings faked with styled `<div>`s, broken `aria-describedby` IDREFs | | **3.1.1 Language of Page** | Missing `lang`, and Spanish-language content inheriting `lang="en"` | Expect the **manual** yield to be dominated by a different set, invisible to automation: **2.4.3** (focus order and restoration), **2.4.7** and **2.4.11** (focus visibility and obscuring), **4.1.3** (announcements that never happen), **2.2.1** (timeout), **3.3.7** and **3.3.4** (multi-step form behavior), **2.5.3** (label in name), and **1.4.10** (desktop-only functionality). These are the findings that justify the audit's cost, and they are the ones a scanner-only audit would have missed entirely. --- ## 15. Every page and state in the frozen sample has been evaluated by every test type its tier requires (§6.1), with evidence recorded. 2. Every WCAG 2.2 Level A and AA criterion has a documented verdict for every sampled page. No blanks. No "Not Evaluated" outside Level AAA. 3. Every finding carries all fields in §13.1, including an independently-assigned severity **and** conformance verdict. 4. Every CRITICAL finding is either remediated and re-verified, or documented in the ACR with a dated remediation commitment. 5. All 8 shared components have been audited once deeply and parity-checked on every host page, with divergences recorded as their own findings. 6. The complete application process has been traversed end-to-end on at least four AT configurations including **both** mobile screen readers. 7. Third-party components are documented with version, observed behavior, affected criteria, current mitigation, and remediation position. YouTube caption/transcript/AD obligations appear in the **agency** remediation backlog, not as third-party exceptions. 8. Inter-rater agreement on SC attribution was measured and met the ≥80% gate before independent work, and was re-measured at midpoint. 9. The ACR names WCAG-EM and its version, lists tool and AT versions, enumerates the sampled URLs, records the random-sample seed, and states that the claim is bounded by the sample. 10. No Lighthouse score, no percentage-conformance figure, and no best-practice finding appears in any conformance table. 11. Every "Partially Supports" carries remarks stating what fails, where, and the user impact. 12. A dated remediation roadmap is published alongside the ACR for every open finding. **Per-finding acceptance for re-test:** a finding is "verified fixed" only when re-tested with the same tool/AT and version, on the same page and state, following the original reproduction steps, with evidence captured. A developer's assertion that a fix landed is not verification. --- ## 17. a11y-Critic Review Checkpoints | Checkpoint | After | Focus of the review | |---|---|---| | 🔍 **1** | WP1 — Pre-flight | Is the sample defensible under WCAG-EM? Risks, Failure Modes, and What This Plan Does Not Claim ### 18.1 Risks | Risk | Impact | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Test environment and seeded data not ready in W1 | Blocks ~60% of the audit | Named owner and W1 hard gate; escalate on day 3 if unmet | | reCAPTCHA blocks automated authenticated runs | Blocks the entire automated authenticated lane | Test keys configured in W1 (§1.7 item 5) | | Remediation not staffed separately | Timeline collapses | Confirm dev capacity **before** W1, in writing. If unavailable, re-plan around a "publish accurate ACR with open items" outcome | | CRITICAL blockers found late in the application flow | Cannot fix before deadline | Tier 1 starts in W4, not W8, specifically to surface these early | | Scope creep from PDFs discovered mid-audit | +40 h unbudgeted | Resolve in W1 (§1.7 item 2); if in scope, extend or explicitly document exclusion | | Two engineers producing inconsistent verdicts | Internally contradictory ACR | Calibration gate + decision log + second review on all CRITICAL and all favorable verdicts (§13.2) | | Pressure to "score the VPAT green" | Legal and reputational exposure | §18.2 | ### 18.2 The failure mode that matters most If the audit finds CRITICAL blockers that cannot be remediated in 13 weeks, there are exactly two honest options: **publish an accurate ACR with open "Does Not Support" rows and a dated remediation roadmap**, or **delay publication**. There is no third option. A knowingly favorable VPAT is a misrepresentation in procurement and, for a benefits portal serving people with disabilities, direct ADA exposure. Agree this position with leadership **in Week 1**, before anyone is emotionally invested in a green report. That agreement is itself a deliverable of WP1. ### 18.3 Negative space — what this plan does not claim - **It does not claim the site conforms.** It produces evidence bounded by a defined sample. Conformance beyond the sample is not established, and the ACR must say so. - **It does not cover native mobile applications, kiosks, or hardware** — Chapter 4 and most of Chapter 5 are "Not Applicable" by assumption, pending §1.7 item 6. - **It does not cover non-web documents unless §1.7 item 2 brings them in scope.** If PDFs are excluded, that exclusion is a stated limitation of the conformance claim, not a silent omission. - **It does not establish usability for people with disabilities.** WCAG conformance is a floor. A site can pass every criterion and still be exhausting to use. Usability testing with disabled users is a separate, and for a benefits portal, strongly recommended activity that this plan does not include. - **It does not cover cognitive accessibility beyond what WCAG 2.2 AA requires** — plain language, reading level, and task complexity in a six-step benefits application are substantial real issues that the AA criteria only partially address. - **It does not guarantee remediation.** It produces findings, priorities, and verification. Fixing them requires development capacity this plan does not control. - **Automated tooling coverage figures cited in §5.2 are estimates**, not measurements of this site. Do not plan capacity as though a specific percentage is guaranteed. --- ## Contract Appendix ### Architecture Overview A WCAG-EM–grounded, risk-tiered audit. Semantic structure and shared-component behavior are specified up front as explicit pass criteria (§3, §4, §7–§10), so two engineers of differing experience produce comparable verdicts. Automated scanning establishes breadth across ~48 page-states; manual keyboard, DOM verification, and multi-platform screen reader testing establish the depth that automation cannot reach. Shared components are audited once and parity-checked everywhere, which is the efficiency that makes the timeline viable. Findings carry severity and conformance verdict as independent fields, preventing the most common category of VPAT inaccuracy.
